excerpts.text:
### Assignment and final compatibility

The Chief belongs to the unanimous vacatur coalition and assigns the coordinated opinion to Stevens. Fit governs: the Associates' sufficient ground is already settled. Stevens's Landgraf/Rivers authorship directly demonstrates the central work of separating new consequences for completed conduct from future regulation; his Lawrence concurrence supports a case-specific equitable assessment rather than enactment-only relief. His reconciled commitment now accepts this bounded remand, and the opinion preserves the matured-claim and practical-danger concerns that made the temporal/remedial distinction necessary. Souter's joins in those cases and Stone's precise approved remand are strong alternatives, but Stevens has the closest demonstrated authorship on the difficult temporal boundary. His initial DIG preference is superseded and creates no present obstacle; authorship does not invent a new circulation conversion. No historical author is imported. The preceding-term assignment baseline reports 101 named Chief assignments, maximum 27 to O'Connor, so the consecutive-term ceiling bars no author. This earliest OT1996 Court opinion is Chief assignment 1 and Stevens's first; it counts once.

Final compatibility: all eight Associates retain the ready reconciliation's vacatur vote and bounded ground. Stevens and Ginsburg's prior DIG objections were resolved at reconciliation, not by exposure to Stone. The present opinion expressly weighs the asserted danger and preserves matured/reparative and independent claims, so their remaining boundaries are met. O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Breyer receive probability plus independent equities, not enactment-only vacatur. Scalia and Thomas join the actual-enactment disposition and its case-specific sufficient ground without adopting Lawrence's disputed agency-advocacy extension or the Landgraf majority's general organizing method. The opinion references governing temporal law and reserves application; it does not require those broader joins. Nine judgment votes and nine direct joins support the stated holding. No Marks analysis or new reconciliation audit is required.

## Event
Department of State v. Legal Assistance for Vietnamese Asylum Seekers, Inc., No. 95-1521. Argued October 15, 1996; decided October 21, 1996. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. The decisions under review, 45 F.3d 469 and 74 F.3d 1308, concern the Department's refusal to process immigrant-visa applications in Hong Kong for Vietnamese applicants screened out of refugee status. The question is whether the policy violates 8 U.S.C. §1152(a)(1), and how the intervening enactment of IIRIRA §633 affects the statutory premise, live claims and available relief. The Government seeks vacatur or reversal; respondents seek affirmance or dismissal of the writ as improvidently granted. This is an argued post-grant disposition, not an asylum-eligibility proceeding.

## Opinion Topology
Justice Stevens delivers the opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Its common ground concerns an actual intervening enactment and the specific equities of this remand; it adopts no new rule for changed Executive advocacy. No separate writing issues.

excerpts.text:
## Judgment, opinion formation and assignment

The single final merits disposition concerning both Mannix convictions is vacatur/remand, six votes to three. The result does not mix reversal of one conviction with affirmance of another. All eight Associates' reconciled reach commitments remain intact, and Stone's fallback gives nine votes to reject the party objection and reach. Part I's explanation has eight direct joins; Part II has nine; Part III has five. Stone's method/remedy support is not silently counted as a sixth join in Part III. Stevens's distinct affirmance rationale is not combined with Scalia and Ginsburg to create an exclusive-findings majority. Every controlling rationale has five or more direct joins; no Marks construction is needed.

**Chief assignment:** Stone is in the six-Justice judgment majority and therefore assigns the single coordinated opinion even though he does not join all its reasoning. He assigns it to **Souter**. The common five-Associate method is settled with the express Yates qualification; that is a recorded join boundary, not a numerical or stylistic reason. Souter's own Yates authorship gives him the concrete advantage in explaining the connection between instructional focus, permissible evidence and the actual verdict. His current Brecht/O'Neal joins directly support the burden and remedy. O'Connor, author of current O'Neal, is the strongest alternative for the category and remedial aspects; Stone's approved position supplies the same broad method/remedy objective and fits their separation. Souter offers the stronger fit for the particular method qualification, the principal work distinguishing this case. No new accommodation is manufactured after reconciliation and no supposed draft exchange is narrated. Workload does not decide the assignment.

The preceding-term assignment baseline and mechanically copied actual assignment statements establish 101 named Chief assignments, largest recipients O'Connor 27 and Souter 23; no recipient exceeded half. Current-term LAVAS is Chief assignment 1 to Stevens. This is **Chief assignment 2**, **Souter's first** this term; the current total is Stevens 1, Souter 1, all others 0. No two-consecutive-term concentration ceiling applies. No historical per curiam authorship is imported. Supplied assignment statements, not future case processing, establish the count; Git existence is unverified under the no-Git instruction.

### Exact final compatibility test

| Justice | Part I: party rationale | Part II: classification/category | Part III: method/application/remand | Final judgment and retained objection |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stone-Zsela | No join; threshold disposition by fallback only | Join | No join in additional reasoning; separate approved whole-record/remedy ground | Vacate/remand; no new factual or qualification choice attributed |
| Stevens | Join | Join | Refuse | Affirm; proper Chapman already fails on this record despite the lower formula's excessive generality |
| O'Connor | Join | Join | Join | Vacate/remand; exact method correction, no present harmlessness finding or equation of knowledge and purpose |
| Scalia | Join | Join | Refuse | Affirm; omitted-purpose harmlessness requires the actual-findings connection, not independent appellate certainty |
| Kennedy | Join | Join | Join | Vacate/remand; apply current category without rewriting his earlier O'Neal ground |
| Souter | Author | Author | Author with the express Yates condition | Vacate/remand; overwhelming evidence or assumed consideration of omitted purpose is insufficient |
| Thomas | Join | Join | Join | Vacate/remand; existing category governs, no universal habeas Chapman rule or invented earlier dissent rationale |
| Ginsburg | Join | Join | Refuse | Affirm with Scalia's actual-findings ground; no adoption of his historical Part II |
| Breyer | Join | Join | Join | Vacate/remand; integrated actual-effect inquiry preserves impeachment, rebuttal, alternative inferences and possible same result |

No post-reconciliation Associate commitment changes. Part III includes the substantive Yates condition required by Souter and accepted by the other four. The condition is neither diluted to overwhelming evidence nor transformed into a finding that this jury considered the missing purpose. The threshold resolution remains the eight-Associate adjudicative acceptance of repeated appellate identification, not a new neutral fact or automatic cure from a rule whose timing predicate is unproved.

## Event
California v. Roy, No. 95-2025. Summary merits disposition, November 4, 1996. On petition for a writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, reviewing its en banc habeas judgment in Roy v. Gomez, 81 F.3d 863. No oral argument is held in this Court. The questions concern whether omission of an aider and abettor's purpose to facilitate robbery is structural or trial error, the harmlessness burden and permissible method on federal habeas, and the antecedent objection that the named petitioners were not parties below. California seeks vacatur or reversal; Roy seeks rejection of review or retention of the habeas-relief judgment.

The trial charge required knowledge of the perpetrator's unlawful purpose and affirmative assistance, excluding mere presence, but omitted Roy's purpose to facilitate the robbery. The jury returned Mannix robbery and first-degree felony-murder convictions and a knife-possession finding without personal knife use. It also convicted Roy of Clark second-degree murder with personal knife use and acquitted him of Clark robbery. The state court reversed robbery-murder and multiple-murder special circumstances and their sentence while otherwise affirming. This federal challenge concerns only the two Mannix convictions. The state and district courts found harmlessness through their functional-equivalence assessments; the en banc Ninth Circuit expressly reached the contrary Chapman conclusion before its separate collateral-standard analysis.

| Opinion of the Court, Part III | Souter | O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer | Vacatur and remand | Qualified actual-verdict method, application limits, preservation and remand directions |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Supports vacatur and remand; joins Part II only | His whole-record Chapman and conditional-relief ground; no join in Parts I or III |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Stevens | No other Justice | Would affirm; joins Parts I and II | Record-specific failure of the State's Chapman showing without an exclusive-findings rule |

Stone-Zsela agrees with rejection of the party-status objection without adopting its rationale. Five Justices directly join Part III; the judgment's sixth vote does not enlarge that opinion coalition.

### Assignment and final compatibility

The Chief joins each unanimous judgment component and assigns one coordinated opinion to Kennedy. Fit controls, with no unresolved necessary accommodation. Kennedy's own Presley opinion supplies the direct-voting/internal-governance distinction, and his Clark opinion supplies the precise nonuse, submission and remedial separation this case requires. His Morse private-association distinction is fully compatible with this governmental County; his Johnson disagreement is preserved as disagreement with governing law, not made a new defect in the temporary plan. Souter's Morse opinion and Stone's detailed approved construction are strong alternatives, but Kennedy has demonstrated authorship on both central established boundaries and can carry the new enact/administer construction within them. Historical Lopez authorship supplies no evidence. The prior-term baseline has no recipient over half, so no concentration ceiling excludes Kennedy. This is one Chief assignment to Kennedy; its chronological ordinal remains for parent integration after Roy. The concurrence adds no Court assignment.

Every Associate joins Parts I–IV exactly as limited above. The narrow public-government rule answers Scalia and Thomas's Morse objections without changing their private-association views. Preserving coverage, merits and remedial authority as separate questions meets Kennedy, O'Connor, Souter and Thomas's boundaries. Preserving the actual temporary plan as an option while withholding automatic validity answers Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer's concern and is supported by the governing Johnson rule. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas apply Johnson without joining its underlying constitutional rationale anew. Stone's complete County-duty, exact-submission, nonuse and independently supported temporary-remedy position fits the shared text. His additional facial-constitutional answer and exact material-policy formulation are recorded separately because the freeze does not establish eight Associate joins to those additional propositions. No silent Stone component needs fallback. All nine vote to reverse and remand; all nine directly join every Court holding. No Marks aggregation or post-reconciliation commitment change occurs.

## Event
Lopez v. Monterey County, No. 95-1201. Argued October 8, 1996; decided November 6, 1996. On appeal from the three-judge United States District Court for the Northern District of California. The court authorized March 1996 municipal-court elections under a countywide, at-large system without preclearance of all operative changes and joined California for further litigation about the source of the system. Review concerns whether a covered County must preclear state-mandated changes despite having no policy discretion; the direct voting change, designation and prospective-laches defenses; and the limits on an enforcement court's use of an unprecleared governmental plan and a wholly court-developed temporary remedy. The plaintiffs seek reversal, prospective nonuse and lawful preclearance or interim proceedings.

## Opinion Topology

Its Parts I–IV correspond to the four controlling holdings below. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela files a concurrence, joined by no other Justice, adding his constitutional response to the designation objection and specifying his boundary for a wholly judicial plan.

Scalia is the strongest alternative for the statutory text; Stevens is a strong alternative for NCIR and temporal architecture. Neither supplies a necessary accommodation absent from Souter's already supported common formulation. Stone's fixed position can state the merits rule, but provides no special drafting advantage over Souter's directly relevant administrative-law work, and is silent on the new threshold reasons. ## Event

INS v. Yueh-Shaio Yang, No. 95-938. October Term 1996. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. Argued October 15, 1996; decided November 13, 1996.

The INS seeks reversal, and Yang seeks affirmance of the restriction on discretionary consideration. The question is whether former §1251(a)(1)(H) permits consideration of immigration fraud connected with and extending beyond the entry fraud that made the applicant deportable. ### Assignment and final compatibility

The actual reversal/remand coalition consists of O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Stone's approved formal judgment is vacatur/remand; Stevens would affirm. The Chief therefore does not assign the opinion for the reversal judgment. O'Connor, the most senior participating Associate in that coalition, assigns it to herself. Her Bostick authorship directly equips her to explain objective encounter classification without a categorical warning or seizure substitute; her Ornelas authorship provides demonstrated care separating supported facts and legal sufficiency, while the opinion respects Scalia's limit against converting Ornelas into a universal consent-review rule. Her Whren and Evans positions support the threshold and objective-motive correction. Kennedy's Evans opinion and Thomas's Whren opinion provide strong alternatives, but the core unresolved encounter problem particularly fits O'Connor's authored Bostick analysis. Ginsburg's separate state-law explanation does not require a new necessary accommodation to obtain the six direct whole-opinion joins. This is an Associate assignment, adds zero to the Chief's census, and does not impose the Chief's preferences on the assignor. Historical Robinette authorship and joins are not assignment premises.

The six whole-opinion Associates retain all reconciled limits: O'Connor requires the actual transition and trial findings; Scalia declines a universal Ornelas extension; Kennedy preserves Mimms's duration boundary; Souter requires a distinct causal inquiry; Thomas rejects both motive-based invalidity and an automatic end-of-seizure rule; Breyer preserves supported findings without conviction reinstatement. The draft satisfies all six without inventing a circulation revision. Ginsburg remains a judgment-only concurrence, accepts the identified legal correction and explains state-law freedom; she is not promoted to a Court-opinion join. Stevens's reconciled merits affirmance is preserved, with his account of the actual record and no-script agreement. Stone's formal vacatur is preserved as a separate remedy, and his direct joins are limited to approved rules and remand inquiries. The standing fallback supplies his exercise-of-review vote on the unaddressed Long component and his disposition-only agreement to set aside the unaddressed motive-based exit-order ground; it adds no explanation and does not convert his overall remedy to reversal. Public Projection preserves these exact limited agreements without exposing the private approval mechanism. Arithmetic: 7 reverse/remand, 1 vacate/remand, 1 affirm; 9 participate. Parts I/II.A have 6 direct joins; II.B/III and the remand framework have 7. No Marks analysis, new factual finding or changed non-Stone commitment occurs.

## Event
Ohio v. Robinette, No. 95-891. Argued October 8, 1996; decided November 18, 1996. On writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court of Ohio. Ohio seeks reversal of suppression and reinstatement of the conviction; Robinette seeks affirmance or a totality-based remand. The questions concern a categorical warning that a traffic detention has ended, the actual transition to a consensual encounter, and validity of consent. The Ohio judgment invoked the Fourth Amendment and Article I, §14 of the Ohio Constitution, held the detention unlawful and unattenuated, and separately imposed a release-warning rule. Both grounds are before the Court.

## Opinion Topology
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | O'Connor | Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Breyer | Reversal and remand | Entire opinion: Parts I–IV |
| Partial joins in the Court opinion | Stone-Zsela | — | Would vacate and remand | Part II.B, objective continued-detention inquiry; Part III, no mandatory federal script and totality consent; Part IV's remand inquiries and limits, excluding reversal as the formal disposition |
| Opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Vacatur and remand | Preserves actual encounter analysis and his distinct formal remedy; adds no ground on Part I or Part II.A |
| Opinion concurring in the judgment | Ginsburg | No other Justice | Reversal and remand | Accepts review under Long and the federal no-script/totality correction; emphasizes independent Ohio law and reserves actual search validity |
| Dissent | Stevens | No other Justice | Affirmance of suppression | Accepts review and rejects an indispensable federal script, but finds continued unlawful detention and no attenuation on this record |

Parts I and II.A have six direct joins. Part II.B, Part III and the identified remand framework in Part IV have seven direct joins. Ginsburg's judgment concurrence and Stevens's agreement on the absence of a federal script are not counted as whole-opinion joins. No controlling rationale depends on combining separate opinions.

## Assignment and opinion formation

The Chief is in each prevailing judgment coalition, including the individual-remand components on which he does not join every rationale. He assigns the single coordinated opinion to O’Connor. The actual shared grounds are settled before author selection: narrow process invalidity; the six-Justice supported educational-interest rule; the eight-Justice bounded institutional correction; eight-Associate proof, statutory-intent and punitive reasoning; and the nine-Justice remedy reservations. No author is selected to induce an additional vote, and no non-Stone commitment changes.

Fit favors O’Connor’s own Croson opinion and Wygant concurrence: they perform the precise evidence, governmental-purpose, individual-burden, alternatives and remedial-fit work needed to distinguish a possibly compelling educational objective from an unconstitutional admissions implementation. Her Metro dissent distinguishes individualized higher-education diversity from a racial viewpoint proxy. Her present commitment supports every Court part without an unresolved accommodation. Souter is the strongest alternative for precedent scope and institutional remedy through his actual Adarand concurrence and Jenkins authorship. Stone is a serious alternative for practical operation and separating injury from remedy, but his additional operational/repair conditions and unadopted proof quantum would require more partial principal-opinion sections. O’Connor’s already shared scrutiny-and-fit formulation offers the concrete coordination advantage. This is fit, not an invented expansion history or a workload quota.

The assignment-only baseline and terminal preceding-term source statements establish 101 named Chief assignments in OT1995, maximum O’Connor 27 and Souter 23. No recipient exceeded half, so the two-term ceiling disqualifies no author here. This event adds one named Chief assignment to O’Connor on promotion; its ordinal must follow the genuinely completed earlier OT1996 assignment statements. None was available at draft assembly. No Git check occurred. Prior assignment-only extracts supply no substantive law or Justice position.

## Event

**Case:** Hopwood v. Texas, October Term 1996; Fifth Circuit No. 94-50664, 78 F.3d 932, reviewing the judgment at 861 F. Supp. 551. Merits decision, November 25, 1996. On review of the Fifth Circuit’s judgment of March 18, 1996; rehearing denied April 4, 1996. No argument date or separate Supreme Court docket number is established in this account.

**Questions:** Whether racial and ethnic educational diversity can be a compelling interest in public-university admissions; whether race-conscious preferences may remedy past discrimination and what predicate and necessity must be shown; and whether the law school’s 1992 system was constitutional and what relief the affected applicants may obtain. The related intervention appeal, No. 94-50569, is outside the grant.

**Record and posture:** Four white Texas applicants—Cheryl Hopwood, Douglas Carvell, Kenneth Elliott and David Rogers—challenge the 1992 process in an individual, nonclass suit. They sought declaration, injunction, admission, compensatory damages and punitive damages under the Equal Protection Clause, §§1981 and 1983 and Title VI. The named defendants include State entities and officials in their official capacities. The District Court found the separate discretionary-review machinery unlawful, awarded one dollar nominal damages to each applicant, declaratory relief and fee-free reapplication, and refused compensation, punitive damages, admission and a broad injunction. The Fifth Circuit remanded individual causation under a school-borne preponderance burden, rejected diversity and the offered remedial grounds, retained the punitive and injunction denials, and left Eleventh Amendment immunity undecided.

In March 1992, resident presumptive-admit index thresholds were 199 for white and other nonpreferred applicants and 189 for Black and Mexican-American applicants; presumptive-deny thresholds were 192 and 179. Earlier preferred-group thresholds varied. Score categories admitted exceptions: some presumptive-admit files moved to discretionary review, and some low-score files could move upward. The preferred groups had separate discretionary review and waiting lists. Enrollment aspirations and observed percentages were not proved fixed reserved seats. How different waiting lists were compared for final places is not fully established. Hopwood’s 199 index led to discretionary review after an assessment of her educational background; the other applicants had indexes of 197. The later program changed the old arrangements, but its full operation is not before the Court.

DeAngelis v. El Paso Municipal Police Officers' Association; Fifth Circuit No. 93-8700. Argued October 15, 1996; decided January 6, 1997. ## Event

United States v. Watts; United States v. Putra, No. 95-1906. Submitted without oral argument on a single Rule 12.4 petition; decided January 6, 1997. The petition seeks review of separate Ninth Circuit judgments vacating the defendants' sentences, 67 F.3d 790 and 78 F.3d 1386. The question is whether a general acquittal categorically bars consideration of the underlying conduct in mandatory Guidelines sentencing, including the distinct statutory, double-jeopardy, due-process and jury-allocation objections.

Watts was convicted of possessing cocaine base with intent to distribute and acquitted of using a firearm in relation to a drug offense. Cocaine base was found in a kitchen cabinet and loaded guns and ammunition in a bedroom closet. The judge found firearm possession connected to the drug offense by a preponderance and applied the two-level §2D1.1(b)(1) adjustment. Putra was convicted for involvement in a one-ounce cocaine transaction on May 8, 1992, and acquitted of the corresponding charge involving five ounces on May 9. Both were videotaped. The judge found her involvement in the second transaction by a preponderance and aggregated the quantities under §1B1.3. Each court of appeals judgment rested on a categorical prohibition against the challenged acquitted-conduct use. Each preserved sentencing objection and each judgment receives separate treatment.

Souter's Williamson join and Stone's complete comparative-value formulation are strong alternatives. ## Event

Old Chief v. United States, No. 95-6556. Argued October 16, 1996; decided January 7, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, which affirmed the federal conviction. The question is whether Rule 403 permitted the Government to identify the name and nature of a prior assault conviction solely to prove felon status when Old Chief offered to admit the complete qualifying status element.

The charges arising from a 1993 confrontation included assault with a dangerous weapon, use of a firearm in a crime of violence and possession of a firearm by a prohibited person under §922(g)(1). The prior judgment described a December 18, 1988 assault causing serious bodily injury and a five-year sentence. Old Chief offered an admission, moved to exclude the name and nature, and renewed his objection when the judgment was introduced. The prosecutor refused the stipulation, and the judge accepted that refusal on the prosecution's general freedom to choose evidence. The jury convicted; the Ninth Circuit upheld the evidentiary ruling without deciding harmlessness. The preserved judgment-record objection is distinct from the requested and later withdrawn credibility instruction. The proposed status instruction required clarification of legal adequacy, but that was not the trial court's ground for refusing the offer.

## Event

Walmer v. Department of Defense; Tenth Circuit No. 93-3377. Argued October 16, 1996; decided January 13, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the Tenth Circuit, which affirmed denial of a preliminary injunction and dissolved its appellate stay on April 4, 1995, 52 F.3d 851. The questions concern equal protection under the Fifth Amendment, the role of military deference, and the Bill of Attainder Clause in separation under the earlier executive Army Regulation 635-100.

Major Joyce Walmer admitted the past homosexual acts on which the Board of Inquiry proceeded and expressly stipulated that she did not qualify for the regulation's retention exceptions under paragraphs 5-51a(1)–(5) and 5-56. Other initial allegations, including a same-sex marriage, marijuana use and conduct unbecoming, were excluded from the Board proceeding and supply no alternative basis here. The district court decided likelihood of success without finding irreparable injury, comparative harm or public interest. The court of appeals assumed those other factors only for its modified likelihood inquiry, under which serious, substantial, difficult and doubtful merits questions could warrant deliberate investigation if the remaining factors were satisfied. That assumption was not a finding that they were satisfied. ## Assignment

**Assignment authority:** The Chief supports every judgment component and assigns the single lead. Its form, governing propositions and part-specific joins were fixed before the source-table recount.

**Counts before assignment:** Stone-Zsela 4; Stevens 4; O’Connor 9; Scalia 4; Kennedy 4; Souter 8; Thomas 4; Ginsburg 5; Breyer 4. The actual Record-table recount is `tmp/COUNT_BEFORE_BROWN.json`. **Last counted event:** Nabozny v. Podlesny, March 10, 1997.

**Eligible authors:** Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer directly support every part. Stone is ineligible for the entire lead because his standing fallback supplies no Part III mixed-motive reason. His full support for the other parts does not authorize division when an eligible Associate can carry the complete opinion. **Balance pool:** Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer, counts four or five, at most one above the eligible minimum of four. O’Connor and Souter remain eligible but outside the pool.

**Author chosen:** Stevens. Fit governs because the precise limited opinion already has the necessary direct joins. Its central work is to enforce Beadle’s supported-burden inquiry without repeating the lower court’s actual-disruption-only language, distinguish statutory accommodation from religion-specific constitutional excess, and preserve the existing mixed-motive liability/remedy allocation. Stevens’s Beadle and NTEU opinions and his Price Waterhouse participation demonstrate the relevant work across those specific questions. His stronger establishment concerns remain within the frozen scope: the opinion does not declare all supervisor-led prayer private or constitutional. Breyer is the strongest eligible pool alternative because his Andrade and Wright opinions carefully separate actual authority, burdens, proof and remedial posture. Stevens has the more direct demonstrated formulation experience with the operative accommodation standard and prospective speech burden; neither count nor authorship creates a new join. Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg remain fully capable and eligible, with no identified necessary accommodation that makes one of them the stronger choice. Stone is not compared as an eligible alternative because his Part III reason is absent, not because of subject-matter ability, office or prior count.

**Final compatibility:** Each Associate joins all four parts at the reconciled scope. Stone joins Parts I, II and IV, concurs in Part III’s disposition through fallback, and adds only his separate attribution/speech account. Statutory liability remains closed, the relief-only tracks remain distinct and no constitutional termination claim is added. No Associate commitment changes in assembly and no reassignment is needed.

## Event

Brown v. Polk County; Eighth Circuit No. 93-3313, 61 F.3d 650 (en banc). Argued November 13, 1996; decided March 17, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. Its en banc judgment issued July 31, 1995, and rehearing was denied August 21, 1995.

After a five-day bench trial, the District Court ruled for the County and its officials. The en banc court reversed the statutory religious-discharge judgment and the judgment on the two actually argued constitutional restrictions, remanding for appropriate relief; it affirmed the separate statutory race judgment. Review concerns religious accommodation, the breadth of the religion-specific directives, public-employer authority and the asserted operational and Establishment justifications.

Isaiah Brown directed the County’s information-services department. The record separately identifies secretarial typing of Bible-study notes, prework office prayer, voluntary and irregular department-meeting prayers, and a single religious work-ethic reference. The County ordered an end to activities characterized as witnessing, proselytizing or counseling and removal of religious items, including a desk Bible. Statutory claims challenge the later discharge; the constitutional claims actually argued challenge the reprimand and removal order, not termination.

## Assignment

**Assignment authority:** The Chief joins the affirming judgment coalition and its full confined ground and assigns the single signed lead. The seven-Justice form and limited tax rationale were established before the recount; the broader valuation theory was excluded on the merits of the frozen join barriers, not to alter counts.

**Counts before assignment:** Stone-Zsela 4; Stevens 5; O’Connor 9; Scalia 4; Kennedy 4; Souter 8; Thomas 4; Ginsburg 5; Breyer 4. The actual Record-table recount is `tmp/COUNT_BEFORE_HUBERT.json`. **Last counted event:** Brown v. Polk County, March 17, 1997.

**Eligible authors:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; each directly supports the whole confined opinion. Stone’s current approved tax position, not fallback, supplies eligibility. Scalia and Breyer dissent. **Balance pool:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg, with counts four or five, no more than one above the eligible minimum of four. O’Connor and Souter are eligible but outside the pool.

**Author chosen:** Kennedy. Fit governs because the six reconciled Associate joins and Stone’s approval already support this exact qualified rule; no necessary new join or unresolved formulation objection remains. The actual writing task is to give the Commissioner’s regulatory construction its governing deference while enforcing the material-limitation text, separate qualification from valuation, and tie affirmance to the precise litigation burden without announcing a universal method. Kennedy’s Thomas Jefferson University and Auer opinions demonstrate that text-and-actual-ground work across detailed regulatory qualifications. Stone is the strongest pool alternative: his current supplement gives a precise materiality/burden formulation and expressly reserves valuation timing. Both can write the narrow holding, but Kennedy’s demonstrated execution of the very own-regulation boundaries being applied supplies the concrete comparative advantage. Thomas’s shared materiality/burden position and Stevens’s and Ginsburg’s joins are fully eligible, not discounted by experience or prior authorship; none supplies a necessary new accommodation identifying a different author. Counts remain within the prescribed pool, and no historical Hubert authorship determines this assignment.

**Separate writing:** Scalia writes the common dissent for himself and Breyer because its principal textual claim treats the diversion as a material loss of beneficial net value under the regulation and governing deference. Breyer’s distinct concern about timing, economic equivalence and a possible properly justified simplification is preserved within the summary, without a second document or approval of a dollar-for-dollar formula. This separate writing is not counted.

**Final compatibility:** The written majority states only the seven directly shared propositions. O’Connor, Souter and Thomas’s barrier to a comprehensive valuation-date theory remains respected, as does Stone’s express reservation. Scalia and Breyer retain reduction/remand with calculation reserved. No Associate commitment changes in assembly, no Marks synthesis is used and no reassignment is necessary.

## Event

Commissioner v. Estate of Hubert, No. 95-1402. Argued November 12, 1996; decided March 18, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, which affirmed the Tax Court in Estate of Hubert v. Commissioner, 63 F.3d 1083, affirming 101 T.C. 314.

The question is whether administration expenses paid from postmortem income attributable to marital and charitable residuary bequests require reduction of their estate-tax deductions. Nearly $2 million in expenses was paid from an estate exceeding $30 million: approximately $500,000 from principal and the remainder from income. The estate reduced deductions for principal-funded expenses. The Commissioner challenges the treatment of the income-funded amount. Qualification of the trusts was stipulated; the dispute is valuation.

Before the recount, the opinion’s four parts and eight-Associate full joins were fixed on their own legal grounds. Stone’s separate join scope is retained, and one eligible Associate can carry the whole opinion.

**Counts before assignment:** Stone-Zsela 4; Stevens 5; O’Connor 9; Scalia 4; Kennedy 5; Souter 8; Thomas 4; Ginsburg 5; Breyer 4. The actual Record-table recount is `tmp/COUNT_BEFORE_YOUNG.json`. **Last counted event:** Commissioner v. Estate of Hubert, March 18, 1997, alphabetically preceding Young. Hubert counts for assignment but supplies no intervening law to this uncoordinated same-day peer.

**Eligible authors:** Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer directly join Parts I–IV. Stone’s fallback timely-review vote supplies no Part I reason, so he is ineligible for the whole lead; no extra division of authorship is permitted or needed. **Balance pool:** Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer, with counts four or five, at most one above the eligible minimum of four. O’Connor and Souter remain eligible but outside the pool.

**Author chosen:** Breyer. Fit governs: no unresolved accommodation is needed to preserve the eight full joins. The opinion must distinguish existing community liberty from an unreceived parole benefit and from the nonexclusive state-entitlement route, then preserve Morrissey’s practical administrative stages and the exact original/later-rule sequence. Breyer’s controlling Sandin opinion directly formulated the preserved route on which this opinion relies, and his current frozen commitment keeps that distinction without an unnecessary program-entitlement remand or new process test. Thomas is the strongest lower-count pool alternative, given his Lynce opinion’s distinction between an actual habeas threshold and an unsupported defect; he too can write the complete timing and merits opinion. Breyer’s demonstrated formulation of the direct-liberty/state-entitlement boundary supplies the stronger case-specific fit at equal counts. Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy and Ginsburg are not excluded by experience, historical votes or prior authorship; their full eligibility is retained, and no necessary differing formulation identifies one of them instead. Stone is excluded only by his absent timing rationale, not by capability or office. Historical Young authorship plays no role.

**Final compatibility:** All eight Associates retain the complete rehearing, community-liberty, original/later-rule, ordinary-procedure and bounded-remedy commitments. Stone’s express Morrissey merits support covers Parts II–IV, with final revocation distinguished from lawful interim detention and prompt process. His fallback supplies timely review only. There is no new Associate position, complete-hearing-before-arrest rule, emergency-only detention condition, numerical deadline or automatic release. No separate writing or reassignment is needed.

## Event

Young v. Harper, No. 95-1598. Argued December 9, 1996; decided March 18, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, which reversed the denial of federal habeas relief. The question is whether termination of Oklahoma preparole community release requires the procedures governing revocation of parole.

Harper was released in October 1990 to live at home, work and report to a parole officer under parole-like conditions. After five apparently uneventful months, the Governor denied formal parole; on March 14, 1991, an officer telephoned and directed him to return immediately to prison without the required revocation process. An August 1991 procedure later addressing parole denial postdated that return. The original procedure was silent on the effect of parole denial, and Harper’s acknowledgment tied community status to compliance with release conditions.

The appellate rehearing petition was two days late, but the Tenth Circuit granted leave, treated it as timely and withheld the mandate until denial. Certiorari was sought within 90 days of that denial.

## Assignment

**Assignment authority:** The Chief directly supports the reviewed reversal and remand and assigns the lead. The single signed opinion, its four distinct reviewability propositions, all nine full joins and the preserved NEPA boundary were established before counting or choosing an author.

**Counts before assignment:** Stone-Zsela 4; Stevens 5; O’Connor 9; Scalia 4; Kennedy 5; Souter 8; Thomas 4; Ginsburg 5; Breyer 5. The fresh actual Record-table recount is `tmp/COUNT_BEFORE_BENNETT.json`. **Last counted event:** Young v. Harper, March 18, 1997. Both March 18 decisions also enter law through the separately validated March 19 source.

**Eligible authors:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer directly support the whole governing rationale. The Chief relies on his approved express grounds, not the standing fallback. **Balance pool:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer, each at four or five, no more than one above the eligible minimum of four. O’Connor and Souter remain eligible but outside the pool. One author can carry the complete opinion; no division is warranted.

**Author chosen:** Scalia. Fit governs because no recorded disagreement requires an accommodation to secure or retain the nine full joins. The opinion must enforce concrete personal injury and litigation-stage proof while recognizing that the alleged water loss supplies the personal causal link absent from an abstract procedural grievance; it must then distinguish that constitutional inquiry from each enacted review channel and the provision-specific APA inquiry. Scalia’s own Lujan reasoning demonstrates the relevant separation of personal interest, procedural right and proof stage, and his frozen Bennett commitment applies that separation while giving the citizen-suit text its breadth only within its actual channels. That combination supplies the strongest case-specific fit for the principal standing dismissal and its alternative reviewability grounds.

The Chief is the strongest pool alternative at the same count. His Franklin opinion and his approved Bennett supplement demonstrate a concrete strength in completed agency action, practical legal consequences and separation of reviewability from merits and remedy. He can faithfully carry the entire opinion. Scalia’s more directly demonstrated articulation of the constitutional standing boundary, paired here with his express channel-specific commitment, provides the meaningful advantage for this case; the Chief’s approved objective is fully preserved without a new formulation or selective doctrinal development requiring his authorship. Scalia’s earlier Franklin disagreement is not a barrier: his frozen position accepts this statement’s distinct conditional taking consequences and applies Franklin at its actual controlling scope. Thomas has the same count and full support, but the record identifies no corresponding advantage over the author of the concrete-interest analysis the opinion applies. Stevens, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer remain fully capable pool members; no different accommodation or lower count selects them. No historical Bennett authorship, general stylistic reputation or assumed inability supplies the choice.

**Final compatibility:** All nine retain direct joins to pleaded Article III sufficiency, the distinct citizen-suit channels, provision-specific APA review and completed agency action with conditional taking consequences. The actual Franklin majority and Dalton preclusion holding govern; noncontrolling predecessor rationales are not converted into law. Notice and other statutory prerequisites remain unadjudicated, the designation and biological merits remain open, and the unchallenged NEPA dismissal remains undisturbed. No fallback, changed Associate commitment, invented circulation history or separate writing is needed.

## Event

Bennett v. Spear, No. 95-813. Argued November 13, 1996; decided March 19, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which affirmed dismissal in Bennett v. Plenert, 63 F.3d 915.

The Bureau of Reclamation consulted the Fish and Wildlife Service about the Klamath Irrigation Project and two endangered fish species. The Service’s Biological Opinion found likely jeopardy and identified minimum reservoir levels as reasonable and prudent alternatives; the Bureau stated it would comply. Irrigation districts and ranch operators allege injury from reduced water and challenge the Opinion under the Endangered Species Act and Administrative Procedure Act. The questions are constitutional standing, the scope of the statutory review channels, the provision-specific zone of interests and final agency action. A fourth claim alleging an unassessed de facto habitat designation under NEPA was dismissed below and that dismissal is unchallenged.

## Assignment

The Chief assigns the controlling portions supporting the standing and injunction judgment. Stevens, the senior Associate in the eight-Justice intervention majority, assigns V-A. The shared lead can be assigned to one Justice who supports all its propositions; dividing authorship is unnecessary. Both assign Ginsburg. The Chief's balanced pool governs his portions and the common author.

**Counts before assignment:** Stone-Zsela 4; Stevens 5; O'Connor 9; Scalia 5; Kennedy 5; Souter 8; Thomas 4; Ginsburg 5; Breyer 5. **Last counted event:** Bennett v. Spear, 1997-03-19. The fresh recount reads actual current-term Record opinion tables, including earlier same-day assignments for counting only. Receipt: `freeze/OT_1996CHUNK6_61_ASSIGNMENT.json`; bounded source extract: `runtime/assembly/OT_1996CHUNK6_61_ASSIGNMENT.md`.

**Eligible authors for the whole lead:** Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Each directly supports every controlling proposition; the other four have substantive partial joins or dissents. **Balance pool:** Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer, each five; eligible minimum five. O'Connor nine and Souter eight are outside the pool. Stone's lower count does not cure his withheld pressure and intervention joins, and his fallback supplies no authorship eligibility. He could carry some parts but a whole-opinion author exists, so the no-unnecessary-division rule controls.

**Author chosen:** Ginsburg. Fit, not expansion, governs the settled shared grounds. Her Chabad and Good News positions and Brown join furnish a concrete basis for distinguishing contextual government attribution from protection of private expression while tailoring relief to actual state action. Her frozen commitment also treats the Attorney General's actual representation rather than public identity as dispositive. Stevens is the strongest pool alternative, with direct joins to both Lee grounds and the same count; his Pinette and Good News positions equally support the official-worship boundary. Ginsburg's specific current-term private-expression/remedy position most directly carries the combined task of continuing a narrow restraint while protecting independently lawful speech. Breyer is fully capable and at the same count; no distinct unresolved formulation calls for expansion or an additional part. Stevens's own assignment of V-A is consistent with its shared individualized adequacy ground. No historical authorship is imported.

## Event

**Ingebretsen v. Jackson Public School District**, court-of-appeals No. 94-60631, 88 F.3d 274. Merits decision, March 19, 1997. On review of the Fifth Circuit's affirmance of a preliminary injunction against Mississippi's school-prayer statute, its graduation exception and denials of student intervention. Merits hearing and decision: March 19, 1997 under the established Court calendar; no separate argument date is supplied.

The questions concern preimplementation standing; official versus private student prayer, including school pressure and a statutory disclaimer; lawful reach and severability of interim relief; the graduation exception; and intervention under Rule 24.

| Same opinion, partial joins | Ginsburg | Kennedy | Supports every judgment component | I, III, IV and V; no II |
| Same opinion, partial joins | Ginsburg | Scalia, Thomas | Supports standing and intervention; dissents from retained injunction and graduation extension | I, V, and IV's independently stated protection of private speech and lawful provisions; no II, III or retained-restraint application |

The dissenters join only scope and cannot author the whole lead. **Balance pool:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens and Kennedy; the eligible minimum is four and upper count five. Souter and Breyer are outside the pool. Breyer's withheld independent economic rationale does not exclude him from this actual common lead, which contains no such branch; his count does.

**Author chosen:** Kennedy. His own actual Turner I opinion establishes the precise majority standard and its limits, and his Denver position insists that the separate content classifications cannot be silently sustained. That combination directly fits the present supported-prediction, independent-review and limited-grant explanation. Stone, at four, is the strongest alternative and expressly supports the same review and remedial boundaries; the one-opinion range permits Kennedy at five, and his recorded distinction between the majority standard and the former insufficiency plurality offers the most exact fit. Stevens is also within the pool and fully eligible, with his separate view of the earlier record retained in a concurrence; no refusal to join the present lead is attributed to him. The choice follows the actual earlier opinion and frozen current commitments, not historical Turner II authorship. No pool expansion or artificial additional lead is needed.

## Event

**Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. v. Federal Communications Commission**, No. 95-992. Merits decision, March 31, 1997. Argued October 7, 1996. On direct appeal from the three-judge District Court for the District of Columbia, 910 F. Supp. 734, after the 1994 remand. The granted question asks whether the developed record establishes advancement and fit under the intermediate scrutiny prescribed for the general full-power must-carry core.

**Statutory setting relevant to fit:** Under 47 U.S.C.§534, systems with 12 or fewer usable activated channels must carry at least three local commercial signals; systems also having 300 or fewer subscribers are exempt from that section only while they delete no broadcast signal. Systems with more than 12 channels carry eligible local commercial signals up to one-third of usable activated capacity. This is not a combined commercial-and-educational ceiling. Substantially duplicative commercial signals already represented in carriage and additional same-network affiliates need not be carried; voluntary duplicates and multiple affiliates count toward the obligation. When eligible stations exceed the required number, the operator selects among them, but cannot substitute low power for full power and must choose the elected network's affiliate with the closest city-of-license reference point to the principal headend.

Section535 adds separate educational duties. Systems with 12 or fewer channels carry one qualified local educational signal and may carry more. Systems with 13–36 carry at least one and need not carry more than three, subject to continued carriage; they may carry more. If no qualified local station is present, the former category must import one qualified educational signal and the latter at least one. For that importation, the smallest systems need not remove programming actually provided on March 29, 1990 but must use the first available channel. All qualified local educational stations carried on that date retain carriage unless operator and station give written waiver consent. Systems above36 channels, including those expanding beyond36, carry requesting qualified local educational stations; a system required to carry three need not add stations substantially duplicating another qualified local educational station requesting carriage. This is not a general three-station cap. A13–36-channel system already carrying a State-network educational affiliate need not add another same-network affiliate whose programming substantially duplicates the carried affiliate.

Commercial distant signals require indemnification of increased copyright liability. A commercial station below the specified headend levels (−45dBm UHF; −49dBm VHF) is excluded if it does not agree to bear the costs of delivering a good-quality or baseband signal. Educational carriage is not required without delivery of a good-quality or baseband signal; its distant-signal indemnity exception concerns adding a signal and expressly does not erase the continued-carriage rule. These are actual programming obligations, including primary video, audio and captions. Commercial carriage includes technically feasible program-related blanking-interval or subcarrier material; educational carriage includes technically feasible program-related ancillary material necessary for disability access, education or language purposes. Other ancillary material remains discretionary. Positioning and availability duties also constrain operation; the law does not merely reserve empty channels. No new dispute over ancillary material, positioning, payment, notice or enforcement is decided.

The reserved low-power duty depends on an insufficient number of full-power local commercial stations: systems with35 or fewer channels carry one qualified low-power station, and larger systems two. Its disputed programming criterion concerns local needs inadequately served because of full-power stations' geographic distance. The separate market-modification factor asks whether another eligible station supplies the community news, sports or events; it is not that requirement imposed on the requesting station. These provisions' independent classifications remain outside the granted question.

## Event

Camps Newfound/Owatonna, Inc. v. Town of Harrison, No. 94-1988. On review of the Supreme Judicial Court of Maine, 655 A.2d 876, which on April 21, 1995 reversed summary judgment for the camp and sustained the challenged property tax. Argued October 9, 1996; decided May 19, 1997. The question is whether the nonresident-beneficiary condition in Maine's charitable-property exemption discriminates against interstate commerce and whether a subsidy, market-participant or resident-benefit justification sustains it. The Maine nonprofit's 180-acre Christian Science camp recruits nationally; about 95 percent of campers come from outside Maine. Its reported charge is roughly $400 per week and annual property taxes exceed $20,000. It timely pursued state refund and prospective-exemption procedures.

Section 652(1)(A) generally covers real and personal property owned and occupied or used solely for the purposes of benevolent and charitable institutions incorporated by Maine, without loss of exemption merely because of the source of funds or limitations in beneficiary classes, subject to the express nonresident subparagraph. An institution operated principally for nonresidents may exempt no more than $50,000 of current just property value only if the statutory average weekly charge per person does not exceed $30; above that rate it receives no exemption under that subparagraph. The computation divides all tax-year stipends or charges for services, benefits or advantages by all persons receiving them during that year, then divides by the weeks during that tax year when the institution is actually operated principally for nonresidents; §502 defines the tax year. The reported weekly price is not substituted for that statutory computation.

The nonresident subparagraph does not apply to a nonprofit corporation incorporated solely to conduct medical research; that exception does not waive the general exemption's other requirements and is not found applicable to this camp. The paragraph also includes nonprofit nursing, boarding and boarding-care facilities licensed under Title 22, chapter 1665 or its successor; nonprofit community mental-health facilities licensed under Title 34-B, chapter 3; and nonprofit child-care centers incorporated by Maine as benevolent and charitable institutions. Nonprofit means exempt under Internal Revenue Code §501(c)(3). No independent challenge to Maine incorporation, neutral qualification, religious liberty, equal protection or travel rights is decided.

## Form fixed before assignment

One signed Opinion of the Court follows plenary argument. The constitutional immunity, official-function boundary, integrated-order review and remedial questions constitute one argued case and one connected opinion. A per curiam disposition would not adequately identify responsibility for this reasoned resolution and its distinct published positions. The Court opinion has five parts fixed on legal grounds: I, confined review; II, temporary immunity; III, official-function boundary and reserved defense; IV, present trial stay and its derivative remedy; V, future accommodation and the post-decision standard. The Ferguson consequence remains a remedial paragraph of Part IV, not an independent immunity adjudication or separately assigned opinion.

The judgment coalition is all nine Justices. The Court-opinion coalition is Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg throughout. Breyer concurs in the judgment, substantively agrees with denial of automatic immunity and rejection of the unsupported stay, and preserves his additional Article II qualification without formally joining the Court opinion. His position is not converted into complete assent by the Court's constitutional-respect language.

The eight complete Court-opinion joiners are the eligible authors: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. Breyer's judgment-only relationship excludes him from full lead authorship. No split authorship is warranted because eight authors can carry every part. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela is in every judgment coalition and assigns. This legal form and eligibility were fixed before counts or authorship were considered. The assignment below accounts for all earlier qualifying opinions of this Term.

### Assignment statement

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela assigns the one signed plenary lead opinion to Justice Scalia. The judgment coalition and the five-part legal form were fixed before the count. No proposition, part or case was added, divided or combined for assignment purposes. All eight complete Court-opinion joiners can deliver the whole opinion; Breyer's judgment-only relationship excludes him from that assignment, and there is no reason to divide authorship.

The opinion-assignment count is recorded in [the assignment receipt](../tmp/Clinton_assignment_recount.json). It includes 79 qualifying opinions delivered before this assignment. Dates control, with same-date case names in alphabetical order. The last counted event is Church on the Rock v. City of Albuquerque, May 27, 1997, delivered by Stone-Zsela. That peer is counted for assignment only; it supplies no intervening substantive law for this case. There are 79 counted opinions before this assignment. Authors come from the actual opinion tables rather than prior assignment totals. Summary and per curiam dispositions, procedural actions, source admissions and separate writings are excluded as individually identified in the receipt. No undelivered opinion is counted.

| Justice | Count before assignment | Eligible for complete lead | Balance pool |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Stone-Zsela | 9 | Yes | Yes |
| Stevens | 9 | Yes | Yes |
| O'Connor | 9 | Yes | Yes |
| Scalia | 8 | Yes | Yes |
| Kennedy | 9 | Yes | Yes |
| Souter | 9 | Yes | Yes |
| Thomas | 8 | Yes | Yes |

The eligible minimum is eight, so the pool includes every eligible author with eight or nine counted opinions: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. Fit governs; expansion is unnecessary because the eight share the exact bounded grounds, while the Court does not purport to resolve Breyer's further scheduling objection or secure an additional join from him.

The opinion's work is to identify the protected presidential function, separate that immunity from ordinary stay authority, confine appellate review to the integrated protection order and preserve actual-duty accommodation without inventing a universal procedure. Scalia's Forrester and Antoine joins, Nixon Court join, Plaut dissent and Weiss concurrence support precisely that distinction between constitutional allocation, official function and unsupported procedural enlargement. His commitment expressly accepts the required accommodation and every reservation. He can state the settled common grounds faithfully at the lower count. Thomas is the other eight-opinion candidate; his exact structural method also fits, but Scalia's recorded adoption of Forrester's directly relevant function/identity account supplies the more immediate basis for this opinion's central explanation. This is not a limitation on Thomas's capacity to write it.

O'Connor is the strongest alternative at nine because her Forrester opinion directly develops that functional method. The present coalition already agrees on its application, however, and no formulation obstacle requires her authorship; Scalia can carry that existing method and the same limits at the lower count. Stone's position also separates authority, process and relief, but his distinctive new classification guidance remains outside the Court's adopted rule. Self-assignment offers no necessary accommodation, coordination or precision advantage over Scalia for this narrower opinion. Kennedy's Public Citizen and Reich work likewise supports the distinction but identifies no unresolved objection requiring his higher-count assignment. The case's importance, historical authorship and stylistic reputation play no role. The opinion commands eight complete joins; Stone-Zsela and Breyer file the separate writings stated above.

## Event

Clinton v. Jones; No. 95-1853; 520 U.S. 681. Argued January 13, 1997; merits decision May 27, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, reviewing its January 9, 1996 judgment, 72 F.3d 1354. Jones filed this federal and state-law damages action on May 6, 1994, alleging sexual harassment, assault, conspiracy and other injuries beginning in 1991 when Clinton was Governor of Arkansas. The allegations remain disputed. The complaint also includes post-inauguration statements attributed to the presidential press secretary.

The District Court rejected temporary constitutional immunity and permitted discovery against Clinton and Ferguson, but postponed trial until Clinton left office. The Eighth Circuit affirmed denial of immunity and removed the categorical trial stays. Clinton seeks dismissal without prejudice or postponement through the Presidency; Jones seeks ordinary proceedings. The question is whether separation of powers requires dismissal or postponement of this federal damages action based on alleged unofficial pre-presidential conduct, including whether the existing trial stay can stand under ordinary docket-control authority.

Stone-Zsela's concurrence and Breyer's concurrence in the judgment are designated separate-writing summaries: up to 600 words each. Other controlling explanations: up to 350 words each.

### Form, assignment and census

Form was fixed before counting or choosing an author: a single signed Opinion of the Court resolves two presented constitutional questions on grounds directly shared by five Justices. A per curiam disposition would not appropriately present the distinct inference and expression analyses and their material disagreement. No division of authorship is necessary because all five affirmers support every governing proposition. The additional two-Justice conduct-morality position requires a concurrence; the equality dissent and Stevens-only speech ground require distinct parts of a dissent. Neither form nor scope was selected to affect a count.

The [from-scratch census](../freeze/OT_1996CHUNK10_THOMASSON_ASSIGNMENT_CENSUS.md) derives authors from the [mechanically scoped current-term Record opinion tables and assignment excerpts](../freeze/OT_1996CHUNK10_THOMASSON_ASSIGNMENT_EXCERPTS.md), not from earlier tally statements. It includes earlier dates and alphabetical same-day events before Thomasson, including Records already written in this Run. Signed plenary threshold/remand opinions count; summary, per curiam, filing and order actions do not. Kinman's two lead authors count once each.

| Justice | Count before this assignment |
|---|---:|
| Stone-Zsela | 11 |
| Stevens | 10 |
| O'Connor | 11 |
| Scalia | 11 |
| Kennedy | 11 |
| Souter | 12 |
| Thomas | 11 |
| Ginsburg | 11 |
| Breyer | 11 |

Last counted event: Johnson v. Fankell, June 9, 1997, Scalia. There are 98 qualifying earlier Records and 99 author counts. Eligible full-rationale authors: O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer. Their minimum is 11, so the descriptive balance pool is all five. **Assignment authority and status:** Stone is outside the affirming coalition; O'Connor is its senior participating Associate and assigns. The Chief's balance-pool constraint does not bind this Associate assignment. O'Connor assigns the lead to herself. Her own Walmer ordinary-review analysis, both Heller components and speech-evidence joins support a precise separation of lawful prediction from immunity, and of relevant evidence from punishment for advocacy. This is a case-specific continuity/fit reason, not seniority as an automatic authorship entitlement. No formulation dispute requires expansion assignment or a changed commitment. O'Connor's resulting signed lead adds one to her future count; the separate writings add none. Earlier completed assignments remain untouched.

Stevens's two-part dissent performs the frozen equality and separate speech functions in one writing; its Part I is fully compatible with the other three dissenters' recorded grounds and limited remedy. No dissent-assignment balance rule is imposed. Scalia's concurrence preserves the two-Justice additional ground. No fictional circulation sequence, objection cure or changed join is asserted.

## Event

Thomasson v. Perry, Fourth Circuit No. 95-2185, 80 F.3d 915 (en banc). October Term 1996. Argued February 19, 1997; decided June 9, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the Fourth Circuit's April 5, 1996 judgment affirming summary judgment for the Government and sustaining Thomasson's honorable discharge. No separate Supreme Court docket number is supplied. The granted questions concern the Fifth Amendment equal-protection validity of the statement provision, the First Amendment validity of its use as a discharge ground, and the extent of congressional and military deference. Thomasson seeks reversal, declaratory relief, reinstatement and record correction; the Government seeks affirmance.

After approximately ten years of excellent service, Thomasson wrote four admirals in March 1994 declaring that he was gay and opposing the policy. A two-day Board of Inquiry in May 1994 received his service record, supporting testimony and expert evidence, and unanimously found the statutory presumption unrebutted; a Board of Review agreed. He declined further specific rebuttal. No identified past homosexual act, performance failure, security breach or operational impairment was proved. No exclusion of evidence, forced recantation or denied hearing is established on this record. The challenged route is §654(b)(2), not the distinct act or marriage provisions.

| Concurrence | Scalia | Thomas in full | Both join the Court completely; adds only their permissible conduct-morality ground. |
| Dissent, Part I | Stevens | Stone-Zsela, Souter, Ginsburg in full | Ordinary-rationality equality objection and limited discharge-removal/remand remedy; no independent statutory-error ground. |
| Dissent, Part II | Stevens | No other Justice | Independent as-applied First Amendment ground; Stone-Zsela, Souter and Ginsburg do not join or decide that ground. |

## Opinion form and assignment interface

**Form:** One signed lead opinion after plenary merits review, a separate Stone opinion concurring in the common portions and dissenting from the failure to require trial, and one substantive dissent on both sufficient affirmance grounds. No per curiam, artificial opinion division, consolidation or additional lead is warranted by the case.

**Assignment countability:** Counted.

**Assignment authority:** The Chief belongs to the five-Justice common judgment coalition and assigns the lead opinion for that component. The following assignment uses a fresh sequential recount under Engine §8.

**Eligible full-lead authors:** Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Each supports every proposition and the complete remedial accommodation. Stone joins the shared rules, applications and minimum judgment component, but his approved position requires trial and does not support stopping there as lawful and sufficient for his position. He is therefore not eligible to carry the complete lead under §8. The affirming four are outside the judgment coalition. These exclusions concern supported propositions and sufficiency, not capability or style.

**Assignment:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, participating in the common judgment component, assigns the single lead opinion to Stevens. The fresh per-Record counts immediately before assignment are Stone-Zsela 11, Stevens 10, O'Connor 11, Scalia 11, Kennedy 11, Souter 12, Thomas 11, Ginsburg 11 and Breyer 11. Last counted: Johnson v. Fankell, June 9, 1997; Vey's procedural order adds no count and the stopped Thomasson matter supplies no assignment. Full-lead eligibility is Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. The lowest count is 10; the pool is Stevens (10), Ginsburg (11) and Breyer (11). Stevens's Beadle opinion and his actual Brown/Opuku-Boateng joins fit the necessary work of applying the unchanged hardship standard to distinct expressive conduct, separating established distress from conclusive inability to accommodate, and preserving ordinary Rule 56 inferences without guaranteeing a warning or trial. His frozen commitment already contains the complete bounded remand. No changed join or authored compromise is invented. Stone's required-trial position remains separate and does not support the full lead as sufficient; he cannot self-assign that whole opinion. Ginsburg and Breyer can carry the same supported scope, but Stevens offers the stated fit at the lower count. One author can carry every portion, so no division is justified. [Fresh per-Record census](../freeze/OT_1996CHUNK10_ASSIGNMENT_1997-06-12_Chalmers_v_Tulon_Co_of_Richmond.json).

**Separate-writing author:** O'Connor writes the common dissent, with Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas joining. Her own supported managerial-disruption and predictive-hardship application carries both independent affirmance grounds; all four support those grounds without requiring her particular emphasis to become an additional rule. No separate writing is counted under the assignment rule. No circulated draft history or new non-Stone join is invented.

The optional property-specific alternative is omitted from publication because no necessary join depends on it; its frozen support and refusal remain internally preserved.

Britton, June 16, 1997. Kinman's two delivering authors each count once. [Recount](../freeze/OT_1996CHUNK11_ASSIGNMENT_DEL_MONTE.json) and [bounded source extracts](../freeze/OT_1996CHUNK11_ASSIGNMENT_SOURCES_DEL_MONTE.json) preserve the actual tables inspected.

The Chief joins the judgment and assigns. Eligible for the entire lead: Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas, each supporting every Court proposition, including the statutory-language ruling. Stone is not eligible for that complete opinion because he does not supply the statutory ruling; the four dissenters do not support the constitutional jury/application portions. Minimum eligible count is 11; the pool includes all four eligible Justices. Stevens is selected. His Terry concurrence and Tull separate-opinion join supply the action-and-remedy explanation, while his full Markman join makes him particularly well placed to distinguish the present factual tasks without weakening the judge's construction function. Kennedy and Thomas also support the complete ground; Scalia offers a strong statutory-tort account. Stevens carries both that sufficient account and the exact task boundary at the same count, without making the optional property analogy necessary to Scalia's join. No accommodation changes any frozen position and historical authorship supplies no entitlement.

## Event

Del Monte Dunes at Monterey, Ltd. v. City of Monterey; Ninth Circuit Nos. 94-16248 and 94-16313, 95 F.3d 1422; district court No. CV-86-05042-CAL. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1). Certiorari granted January 13, 1997. Submitted and decided June 16, 1997.

Following repeated proposals to develop 37.6 oceanfront acres and the City's final denial, the owners obtained separate takings and equal-protection liability verdicts supporting one $1,450,000 award. The Ninth Circuit's September 13, 1996 judgment sustained the taking claim and the rejection of post-trial relief; it did not reach the City's preserved equal-protection objections. Further appellate and rehearing proceedings were held in abeyance pending this review by a separate appellate order. The grant itself did not remove appellate jurisdiction. The adverse substantive-due-process ruling was not appealed. The owners waived their additional-damages cross-appeal only if the judgment was affirmed.

The questions are whether this §1983 damages action carries a Seventh Amendment jury right on the disputed taking facts; whether the repeated denials can constitute a taking through complete loss of economically viable use or the then-governing substantial-advancement formulation; and whether damages are available through §1983 rather than only prospective or administrative relief. No separate equal-protection merits question is presented.

| Same opinion, V–VII | Stevens | Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas | Supports affirmance | Constitutional jury right, specific factual allocation and supported verdict |
