## Opinion form and assignment

**Form fixed before counting:** One signed lead after plenary merits review, with the three legal subjects stated in Holdings: protected advocacy, the separate personal evidentiary oath, and the bounded further proceedings. The partial Stone join and two separate writings follow substantive differences; neither opinion form nor proposition boundaries was selected to alter eligibility or counts. The frozen F1–F4 propositions remain intact.

**Assignment authority:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela belongs to the unanimous judgment coalition and assigns the single lead. All eight Associates join every proposition. Stone's affirmative approved position, rather than his standing fallback, supports the personal-oath holding and the conditional existing-law remand, but not the complete no-additional-exception advocacy rule. He is therefore ineligible to deliver the entire lead. One eligible author can carry all parts, so no divided authorship is justified.

**Fresh recount:** Actual source opinion topologies are copied in [assignment sources](../freeze/OT_1996CHUNK11_ASSIGNMENT_SOURCES_FLETCHER.json). The recount uses each signed plenary lead once per delivering Justice, in effective-date and alphabetical case-name order. It includes both delivering Justices in Kinman, the signed plenary threshold leads in LAVAS and Lynce, and the earlier same-day Rash, Crawford-El and Del Monte Dunes Records. It excludes Roy's summary disposition, other summary/procedural and unsigned dispositions, admitted sources and separate writings. There are 103 counted opinions and 104 author credits. No earlier assignment tally supplies a count. Last counted: Del Monte Dunes at Monterey, Ltd. v. City of Monterey, June 16, 1997, Stevens.

| Justice | Count before assignment | Eligible for the full lead | Balance pool |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Stone-Zsela | 12 | No | No |
| Stevens | 12 | Yes | Yes |
| O'Connor | 12 | Yes | Yes |
| Scalia | 11 | Yes | Yes |
| Kennedy | 11 | Yes | Yes |
| Souter | 12 | Yes | Yes |
| Thomas | 11 | Yes | Yes |
| Ginsburg | 12 | Yes | Yes |
| Breyer | 11 | Yes | Yes |

**Author chosen:** Stevens. The minimum eligible count is 11, so all eight Associates fall within the minimum-plus-one pool. Fit governs because the eight already share the complete legal ground; no new accommodation is necessary to obtain or retain a majority. The particular drafting work is to distinguish genuine advocacy preparation, supplying evidence, and separate liability predicates without converting either the timing of an act or an allegation of dishonesty into the classification rule. Stevens's Buckley Court opinion already performs the first distinction and preserves genuine advocacy, while his Antoine Court opinion explains the historical-functional justification and the separation of immunity from liability. Applying those two linked rules to one prosecutor's different acts is the principal work of this opinion, and gives him a concrete advantage for this assignment.

Scalia is the strongest lower-count alternative: his Burns and Buckley writings directly analyze the warrant-procuring witness, historical immunity and constitutional injury. He could faithfully write the full opinion at count 11, with his additional historical critique separately stated. Stevens is preferred because his two existing controlling opinions supply the specific paired formulation the Court now applies, including the genuine-preparation qualification important to Kennedy and Souter; this is a fit choice, not an exclusion of Scalia because of his concurrence. Kennedy at 11 has the especially strong trial-preparation distinction in his Buckley writing, but the present opinion must also explain the historical justification and the denial side of the functional boundary. Thomas at 11 supports both relevant functional precedents and the limited historical explanation, and Breyer at 11 supports the practical separation of official-function protection from personal litigation burdens. Each can complete the opinion; neither offers a more direct demonstrated articulation of its combined advocacy/evidence/historical-justification task than Stevens. Ginsburg's Elder opinion strongly fits the reserved legal-defense review, while O'Connor's Hafer opinion fits the personal-capacity distinction, but those are supporting rather than the main new classification work. No historical Fletcher author, later-career evidence, supposed inability or invented circulation exchange determines the selection. The single lead adds one credit to Stevens when counted in later assignments; the separate writings add none.

## Event

*Fletcher v. Kalina*; October Term 1996, chunk 11, inventory No. 119. Ninth Circuit No. 95-36129, 93 F.3d 653, decided below August 22, 1996; no Supreme Court docket number is assigned. Plenary merits review under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1). Submitted and decided June 16, 1997; no separate oral-argument date is established.

Fletcher's personal-capacity §1983 action challenges Kalina's sworn factual certification supporting an arrest warrant. The district court denied absolute immunity and left qualified immunity unresolved on disputed facts; the Ninth Circuit upheld the absolute-immunity denial. Kalina seeks reversal of that ruling. The questions concern whether the personal oath is protected advocacy or the act of a complaining witness, whether preparation and presentation must be separated from factual attestation, and whether allegedly material false statements or omissions contributing to an unconstitutional arrest permit personal liability. The fourth question is reached only to explain the unresolved elements and defenses at this interlocutory stage.

## Opinion Topology

|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Stevens | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer in full; Stone-Zsela joins protection for legitimate charging and advocacy and separation of the personal evidentiary act, but withholds the refusal of an additional knowing-fabrication/deliberate-material-falsehood exception | Eight Justices adopt the complete advocacy-immunity rule and its limit |
| Same opinion, Part II | Stevens | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | All nine adopt the personal-certification holding |
| Same opinion, Part III | Stevens | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer in full; Stone-Zsela joins the unresolved-liability and bounded-remand propositions and accepts existing qualified-immunity law as governing, without an additional ground on the source-specific causation and notice explanations | All nine support the bounded affirmance and remand; eight adopt the complete supporting explanation |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Supports affirmance and remand; proposes the two immunity reforms without altering the governing remand framework |
| Concurrence | Scalia | Thomas | Both join the entire Court opinion; add the limited common-law and stare-decisis explanation |

Her Johnson concurrence directly articulates the statutory remedial accommodation, and her current Hopwood authorship affirmatively recognizes the supported university interest while invalidating the actual means. Piscataway Township Board of Education v. Taxman; Third Circuit Nos. 94-5090 and 94-5112, 91 F.3d 1547 (en banc). On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1). Submitted and decided June 16, 1997.

A necessary reduction eliminated one business-department teaching position. Sharon Taxman and Debra Williams had equivalent qualifications and seniority. Salazar-Haro v. INS; Third Circuit No. 96-3007, 95 F.3d 309. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1). Submitted and decided June 16, 1997.

Pedro Alejandro Salazar-Haro, a Peruvian citizen who entered in 1978 and obtained permanent-resident status in 1983, was convicted in June 1993 of cocaine-distribution conspiracy and aiding and abetting and received forty-two months' imprisonment. His wife and codefendant was deported in 1994; their three sons were United States citizens. The immigration judge considered rehabilitation, remorse, education, employment, care for the children and cooperation with the Government, but denied discretionary relief in light of sustained and renewed trafficking and the admission that he sold more than ten kilograms of cocaine. O'Dell v. Netherland, No. 96-6867. Argued March 18, 1997; decided June 19, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the Fourth Circuit, which sitting en banc on September 5, 1996 reversed the District Court's Simmons ruling under Teague, 95 F.3d 1214. O'Dell's judgment became final on October 3, 1988, after the Virginia Supreme Court's January 15, 1988 judgment. The granted question is whether Simmons's parole-ineligibility protection is available on habeas review of that final capital judgment.

Virginia argued future dangerousness, and the trial court refused the requested parole-ineligibility instruction and an attempted inquiry whether life meant life without parole. The jury found both future dangerousness and vileness and selected death. It also heard O'Dell describe sixteen years on an earlier parole violation and state that, at his age, he would never get out. The District Court's sentencing relief was expressly conditioned on proof of actual legal parole ineligibility; that predicate was not conclusively established by the order.

## Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Stevens | O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | Reject Teague bar | Meaningful-response protection was dictated at 1988 finality |
| Same opinion, Part II | Stevens | Stone-Zsela, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | Independently rejects Teague bar | Even if new, the precisely confined protection qualifies under the watershed exception |
| Same opinion, Part III | Stevens | O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | Formal vacatur and bounded remand | No automatic reinstatement; actual predicates, effect and genuine unresolved habeas conditions remain |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Joins Part II and rejection of the bar; seeks different formal relief | Finds a new rule; would reverse and restore the conditional sentencing-relief framework, with eligibility, effective opportunity and error analysis preserved |
| Dissent | Thomas | Scalia and Kennedy | Would affirm | New procedural rule satisfying neither contemporary Teague exception; no merits or harm finding |

Part I and Part III have five direct joins: Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Part II has five different direct joins: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. O'Connor does not join the watershed alternative. Stone-Zsela does not join the old-rule holding or the exact formal mandate. The two retroactivity grounds are independently sufficient holdings; they are not a synthesis of incompatible rationales.

## Assignment

The single signed plenary original-jurisdiction opinion, its four substantive parts and its implementing-decree directions were fixed on legal grounds before counting. It counts under §8 even though it resolves exceptions to a Special Master's report rather than an appeal. The fresh actual-opinion-table recount gives Stone-Zsela 12; Stevens 14; O'Connor 13; Scalia 11; Kennedy 12; Souter 13; Thomas 11; Ginsburg 12; Breyer 13. Last counted: O'Dell v. Netherland, June 19, 1997, Stevens. The [fresh count](../freeze/OT_1996CHUNK11_ASSIGNMENT_ALASKA.json) and [bounded actual source extracts](../freeze/OT_1996CHUNK11_ASSIGNMENT_SOURCES_ALASKA.json) include all four June 16 additions and the newly entered Klehr, Rambo and O'Dell Records; Kinman's two delivering authors each count once. O'Dell's actual topology and assignment were read in full, and the other 109 counted extracts compared unchanged with the already-read source extracts. The count was recomputed from every actual author cell; no earlier tally supplied it.

The Chief belongs to every judgment coalition and assigns the complete lead. Its eligible authors are Stone-Zsela (12), Stevens (14), O'Connor (13), Kennedy (12), Souter (13), Ginsburg (12) and Breyer (13): each supports all four holdings and the actual decree procedure. Scalia and Thomas support Parts I–II but reject both reservation-title holdings, so they cannot carry the complete opinion. The minimum eligible count is 12; the minimum-plus-one pool is Stone-Zsela (12), O'Connor (13), Kennedy (12), Souter (13), Ginsburg (12) and Breyer (13). Stevens (14) remains eligible but is outside the pool. No division of authorship is needed or justified.

The Chief selects O'Connor. The most demanding work is keeping the separate clear-inclusion and title-defeat inquiries exact while applying different instruments to the Petroleum Reserve and the Range. Her own Utah Division opinion supplies that paired inquiry, and her frozen commitment specifically preserves the difference between §11(b)'s named-reserve treatment and §6(e)'s legally operative wildlife segregation. That is a concrete fit for the opinion's actual work, not an entitlement from historical authorship. Stone is the strongest alternative: his approved position directly supports the strict test, the seasonal-feature limit and the bounded decree procedure, and he is fully eligible at 12. O'Connor's direct development of the controlling two-inquiry standard offers the more specific advantage in answering the express-retention objection without conflating legislative jurisdiction, ownership, geographic inclusion and present legal effect. Ginsburg at 12 can also carry the complete opinion; her full commitment supplies no different accommodation that makes authorship necessary. No recorded disagreement among the seven requires expansion, no Justice is excluded for experience or ability, and no additional join or circulation bargain is invented. The chosen author remains within the required pool and preserves Stone's approved doctrinal limits.

## Event

United States v. Alaska, No. 84, Original. Argued February 24, 1997; decided June 19, 1997. Original action between the United States and Alaska on exceptions to the Special Master's report, not review of a lower-court judgment. The United States filed in 1979 over Beaufort Sea mineral leasing; Alaska counterclaimed to quiet title within the Petroleum Reserve and Arctic Wildlife Range. Hearings and briefing before the Master followed from 1980 through 1986.

The exceptions concern the coastline used for Alaska's Submerged Lands Act grant, Alaska's claimed ten-mile fringing-island rule in Stefansson Sound, Dinkum Sands' island status, and federal retention of submerged lands within the National Petroleum Reserve and original Arctic Wildlife Range. The Master favored the federal position on the first three issues but Alaska on the Range. The 1957 Range application, the pending-application regulation, statehood and the 1960 final reservation are distinct legal events. No final geographic decree is before the Court for entry today.

## Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I–II | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Overrule baseline and Dinkum exceptions | Normal baseline, general-practice and preclusion analysis; Article 10 island criterion and application |
| Same opinion, Parts III–IV | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | Federal title on both reservations | Separate clear-inclusion and title-retention inquiries; congressional confirmation and wildlife segregation; implementing directions |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Thomas | Scalia | Joins Parts I–II; would sustain Alaska's Petroleum exception and overrule the federal Range exception | Express-retention objection under the Submerged Lands Act; pending application is not an established refuge; no join in the unexcepted Range geographic determination |

The complete opinion has seven direct joins: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Scalia and Thomas join Parts I–II only. Their acceptance of decree procedure does not supply a title join or an assent to the Range inclusion determination.

## Event

Agostini v. Felton, No. 96-552, consolidated with Chancellor, Board of Education of the City of New York v. Felton, No. 96-553. October Term 1996, chunk 11, inventory No. 127. The Board and a new group of parents filed motions for Rule 60 relief in October and December 1995. On August 7, 1996, the Second Circuit affirmed denial of relief from the September 26, 1985 permanent injunction implementing Aguilar. The question under Rule 60(b)(5) is whether that continuing onsite prohibition should remain in light of the governing Establishment Clause law and the preserved request to reconsider Aguilar. Fit controls; every proposition already has nine compatible joins, so authorship is not used to manufacture expansion. Scalia's frozen position identifies the central statutory drafting task: preserve Kelley's actual alternatives and the agency interpretation within its lawful text while stating why §1681(b) forbids an imbalance-only preference and does not excuse proved viable unmet demand. Thomas's full join remains unchanged. Stone-Zsela at 13 supports the complete approved equality, scrutiny and institutional-choice framework but is outside the balance pool. Ginsburg at 12 is eligible and in the pool; the recorded statutory-text/deference fit supports Scalia at 11. O’Connor's authorship of Kelley and Virginia does not overcome her exclusion from the current balance pool; those precedents belong to the Court and supply no authorship entitlement.

## Event

Cohen v. Brown University; on writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, No. 95-2205, 101 F.3d 155. Argued May 19, 1997; decided June 23, 1997. Review concerns the three alternative Title IX athletics-accommodation routes, actual unmet interests and the comparative-interest defense, the claimed numerical quota and governmental sex classification, and the scope of equitable relief.

Brown's 1991 restructuring demoted women's gymnastics and volleyball and men's water polo and golf. The District Court entered preliminary protection on December 22, 1992, a merits opinion on March 29, 1995 and final judgment on September 1, 1995. The First Circuit on November 21, 1996 affirmed liability and continuing preliminary protection, vacated the final direction to elevate women's gymnastics, fencing, skiing and water polo to university-funded varsity status, and remanded for another lawful institutional compliance plan. The preliminary two-team relief and later final four-team directive are distinct.

## Opinion Topology

Scalia delivers the unanimous Opinion of the Court, Parts I–III. Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer join throughout. Part I governs statutory accommodation and liability; Part II governs the challenged federal sex classification; Part III governs the distinct preliminary and final remedies. There are no separate writings.

Souter's prior authorship therefore supplies no reason to bypass Stone. Ginsburg at 12 is the lower-count eligible alternative; her complete join and ability to deliver the lead are preserved, while the stated advantage of Stone personally specifying the accepted doctrinal development supplies the self-assignment ground. Breyer at 13 also supports the entire lead and can deliver it; Stevens supports the entire lead at 14 but is outside the pool; no distinctive unresolved accommodation favors one of them. Idaho v. Coeur d’Alene Tribe of Idaho, No. 94-1474. Argued October 16, 1996; decided June 23, 1997. The Tribe alleges federal rights in the beds, banks and waters within the original reservation boundary under an 1873 Executive Order, an 1891 federal statute and an alternative aboriginal-title theory. Its actual prayer seeks exclusive use, occupancy and quiet enjoyment and restraint of state regulatory interference. Review asks whether the Eleventh Amendment bars the prospective officer claims.
